His grandfather told Sami the same story he tells everyone about building the house stone by stone. Sami just chewed on a lemon leaf.

I sat with the women while the men did their thing. Tariq's aunt made sage tea the old way, on a brass tray over coals. It was good. Quiet. I don't mind the errands but she keeps correcting how I arrange the pastries on the tray. Told me that's not how they do it in their family. It's been two years, I still arrange things wrong apparently.

Tariq gave me money to buy a new outfit for Eid. I picked something I liked -- a dark green dress with embroidery on the sleeves. When I showed it to his mother she said it was pretty but maybe something more "appropriate for a young mother" would be better. I don't even know what that means. I put the dress in my closet anyway. I'll wear it.

My own mother sent a voice note about how she wishes I could spend Eid at their house this year. First Eid is always with the husband's family, she knows that, but she said it anyway. So now I feel guilty about being here and guilty about not being there. Sami won't remember any of this. I'm doing all of it for people who have opinions about trays and dresses.", "nudge_response": null}, {"entry_id": "02fb94f3:entry:7", "journal_entry": "Took Sami to the park near the mosque this morning. He's getting better at walking on his own, barely needs my hand now. He kept crouching down to look at ants. We stayed for almost two hours. I didn't bring my phone on purpose.

Ran into Um Fadi from the building. She asked if I was working these days, meaning a real job. I said no, just home with Sami. She nodded the way people nod when they think they're being polite but their face says everything. I used to let that bother me. Today I just picked Sami up and pointed at a bird and we moved on.

Tariq's mother made mansaf for dinner and I helped her roll the jameed. She showed me her mother's technique with the wooden spoon and for once it wasn't corrective, it was like she was sharing something. I actually paid attention. These moments confuse me because they make me forget why I'm frustrated. Or maybe they're exactly why I stay patient through the rest of it.", "nudge_response": null}, {"entry_id": "02fb94f3:entry:1", "journal_entry": "Sami had a fever all night. I was up every two hours. Tariq slept through it. His mother came in at 5am and took over, told me to rest. I should be grateful but it felt like being dismissed. I'm the one who knows what dose of medicine to give, what temperature means we go to the clinic. I didn't rest.", "nudge_response": null}, {"entry_id": "02fb94f3:entry:0", "journal_entry": "My mother-in-law rearranged Sami's entire nap schedule without asking me. She told Tariq it was better for the baby to sleep earlier so she could take him to the park in the afternoon. Nobody asked what I thought. I had finally gotten him into a rhythm that gave me two hours in the evening to work on a logo project. That's gone now.

I stood there in the kitchen holding a cup of tea and I just didn't say anything. Tariq looked at me like he expected me to agree. His mother was already moving the crib blanket to the other room. I could feel my jaw clenching but I smiled. I hate that I smiled. Something about the way everyone just decided felt like they forgot I'm his mother, not a guest in this arrangement.", "nudge_response": null}], "user_phrase": "Honoring the customs and practices I was raised with"}

I said I was interested, which is true, but the whole time I was thinking about how I'd actually handle it. I build things well when people leave me alone to think. That's not what this role is.

retrieval_only_selected.evidence_quote:
Nothing really happened today worth writing about. Spent most of the morning in back-to-back syncs, the usual Monday chaos of catching up on what slipped over the weekend. Ate lunch at my desk again. Kimchi jjigae from the place downstairs, same order for probably the third week running. I keep meaning to try something different but I'm always too rushed to look at the menu properly.

Had a longer-than-expected call with our warehouse partner in Da Nang about the delayed shipment of syringes. Turned out to be a customs paperwork issue on their end. Nothing dramatic. I walked them through it, helped them resubmit. Could've passed it off to my team but I know that particular contact better and it just went faster to do it myself.

After work I sat on the bus home and watched people through the window for a while. Everyone with their faces in their phones. Some guy was asleep with his mouth open, briefcase sliding off his lap. I thought about how we all just do this every day, the same routes, the same tiredness, and nobody really sees each other. Not a depressing thought exactly, just a passing one. Cooked ramyeon at home, watched half an episode of something, fell asleep on the couch.

results.evidence_quote: Came home and made musakhan from scratch, the whole process — rolling the dough, roasting the sumac onions until they were dark and sweet.

My advisor asked today why I chose the topic of hospitality rituals in Levantine households when there are "more contemporary angles" I could take. I told her it was methodologically sound and left it at that. I don't owe anyone an explanation for why this subject matters to me. She's Swedish. She studies migration patterns. The way my grandmother set a table is not something she would understand, and I'm not interested in making it legible to her.

Came home and made musakhan from scratch, the whole process — rolling the dough, roasting the sumac onions until they were dark and sweet. Ate it alone at the kitchen table while my mother watched her show in the other room. The apartment smelled right. That was enough of an answer for one day.

Workshop today. One of the boys, Ahmad, who's maybe twelve, has been coming every week since January. He barely spoke for the first month, just painted the same image over and over, a grey building with no windows. Today he painted a garden. Green everywhere, flowers I don't think he's ever seen in real life, a yellow bird. He didn't say anything about it. He just held it up to dry and went to wash his brushes.

I didn't make a fuss. I just told him the yellow was a good choice and helped him find a spot on the drying rack. It was a small thing. But I drove home feeling like something had actually worked, not because of me specifically, just because the space existed for him to get there on his own. That felt right. I'm exhausted but it's the kind of tired I don't mind.

results.evidence_quote: I got her a proper referral to the physiotherapist and explained everything in simple Dutch, and her daughter translated the rest.
Bought them anyway.

Spent the afternoon at the refugee clinic. There was a Syrian woman, maybe my age, who came in with chronic back pain that's been ignored for months because she keeps getting shuffled between GP practices and nobody follows through. I got her a proper referral to the physiotherapist and explained everything in simple Dutch, and her daughter translated the rest. When she left she squeezed my hand and said something in Arabic I didn't understand but I could tell what it meant.

Those moments remind me why I do what I do. It's not heroic, it's just basic decency — making sure someone gets the care they should have had weeks ago. The system fails these people constantly and most of the time there's nobody there to catch them. I can't fix everything but I can make sure the ones who come through my door don't fall through the cracks.

Walked home along the Maas afterwards and the late afternoon light on the water was beautiful. Felt like myself for the first time all week. Made a simple stamppot for dinner and sat in the garden with a glass of wine and the radio on. Days like this keep me going.

retrieval_only_selected.evidence_quote:
Family group chat exploded today. My uncle Hernando posted a news article about the Guaviare deforestation — same issue the march is about — and wrote "sad but what can you do, these people need to eat." I started typing a response three times. Deleted all of them.

It's not that I disagree entirely — the economics of it are real and I've seen the poverty firsthand. But the framing drives me insane. "What can you do" as if there are no choices, no policies, no one responsible. I wanted to write about the logging companies, the lack of enforcement, the families who actually live there being displaced. But Hernando is my mother's brother and I can already picture the awkward silence at Easter dinner if I go off in the group chat.

So I sent a sad emoji and closed the app. Mature. Professional. Utterly hollow. Patricia would have posted a five-paragraph essay with citations. I admire that and also cannot imagine being that person in my own family. The mural for the march — that I can do. Words in the chat where my grandmother can see them — that's different somehow, and I hate that it's different.

results.evidence_quote: I shut it down, maybe too hard.

Board meeting this morning. Van der Meer had the nerve to suggest we bring in an outside consultant for the digital transformation project. In front of everyone. I built this company when he was still in university, and now he thinks we need some McKinsey type to tell us how to run our own systems.

I shut it down, maybe too hard. Maarten pulled me aside after and said I was "being territorial." Territorial. As if protecting what you've built for thirty years is some kind of character flaw. The company nearly got swallowed six months ago because I trusted people who turned out to be positioning themselves for the takeover. So yes, I'm careful about who gets their hands on strategy now.

She was telling me about the new water heater she got installed and how the plumber tried to overcharge her. I walked her through how to cross-check rates online, sent her a few links. She kept saying "you sound like your father" which — I don't know, it hit different tonight.

After we hung up I checked my bank balance, not because I needed to, just habit. Everything's where it should be. The SIP went through on the 10th, the rent auto-debit cleared, the FD interest got credited. There's something about seeing those numbers line up that lets me breathe properly. I know people think it's boring, the spreadsheets, the tracking, but when I see it all working the way I set it up, it's like — okay, things are holding together.

Spent the rest of the evening ironing my shirts for the week. Put on an old Kishore Kumar playlist. Just felt settled. Not every night is like this but tonight was.
